newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: INTEREST RATE JUMP PUSHES SLOVAK CROWN HIGHER.
newsitem.headline: INTEREST RATE JUMP PUSHES SLOVAK CROWN HIGHER.

text.p: The Slovak crown strengthened slightly in morning trading on Wednesday and dealers said they expected it to move further up on high interbank rates ahead of the minimum reserve deadline on Thursday.
The crown had firmed to some 25 basis points below the midpoint of its mark/dollar basket by 0800 GMT after opening at around -0.30 percent against basket parity.

"We think the crown will strenghten further on purchases by foreign banks which will be attracted by high interest rates on the interbank market," said Brano Matusek, a dealer at Slovenska Sporitelna.
He added the crown could even touch basket parity during the course of the day.
But Andrej Zeman, a trader at the CSOB Bank Slovak branch, said he expected some resistance at around -0.20 percent against the basket midpoint.
"The crown may get stronger throughout the day, but I would say it would move within a range of some -0.20 to -0.60 percent against the basket today and tommorow," Zeman said.
Short-term interbank rates rose to around 30 percent on Wednesday due to a liquidity shortage ahead of the end of the reserve period on Thursday.
O/n funds were trading between 23.00 to 30.00 percent, while one-week rates ranged between 18.50 to 19.25 percent.
"Rates were pushed up by the fact that the banking sector is short of liquidity before the end of the period," said Martin Hrozany, a money market trader at Credit Lyonnais.
According to the central bank, the sector was 0.5 percent short of funds as of May 13.
"The NBS auctioned 3.5 billion crowns in its refinancing repo tender on Wednesday, but the sector needs at least five billion to meet the reserve requirement," Hrozany said.
He added that one-day funds could increase to around 36 percent tomorrow, but that funds up to two-weeks should stabilise below 20 percent at the beginning of the next period.
"(Short-term) rates will go up further on Thursday if something unexpected such as payments for budgetary projects do not add liquidity to the sector, Hrozany said.
